title: Electron- and hole-doped superconductivity in two-dimensional electride ZrX$_2$ (X = Cl, Br, I)
authors: Tian-Xin Liu, Xin-Yang Li, Zuo-Wei Yin, Jing Jiang, Ben-Chao Gong, Wei Fan, Xiao-Le Qiu, Kai Liu
abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) superconducting systems have recently emerged as a frontier in condensed matter physics, driven by their unique physical properties and potential applications. Using first-principles calculations, we show that monolayer ZrX$_2$ (X = Cl, Br, I), which is a family of 2D semiconducting electrides, hosts phonon-mediated superconductivity under both electron and hole dopings. Electron doping in ZrX$_{2}$ can achieve high superconducting transition temperatures at very low concentrations, with ZrBr$_2$ reaching $T_c = 30.0$ K at 0.01 \textit{e}/f.u., followed by ZrCl$_2$ (22.5 K at 0.05 \textit{e}/f.u.) and ZrI$_2$ (18.1 K at 0.01 \textit{e}/f.u.), for which the high $T_c$ originates from the flat conduction band minimum, with Van Hove singularities nearby enhancing the density of states. In contrast, hole doping requires higher concentrations (0.2--0.25 \textit{h}/f.u.) to activate superconductivity, yielding $T_c \sim 2$ K, and approaches a magnetic instability at elevated doping levels. By comparing with InSe and LaBr$_2$, we identify the spatial location and orbital character of excess electrons as key factors determining the strength of hole-doped superconductivity and the nature of competing orders. These findings establish monolayer ZrX$_2$ as a platform for bipolar superconductivity in a 2D electride and provide insights into flat-band engineering for high-$T_c$ superconductors.
summary: This theoretical study uses first-principles calculations to explore superconductivity in 2D electride materials, ZrX2. It demonstrates that electron doping can induce high critical temperatures ($T_c$) due to flat electronic bands, while hole doping results in much weaker superconductivity that eventually gives way to magnetic ordering. The findings establish ZrX2 as a promising, tunable platform for realizing bipolar superconductivity.
main_problem: The study investigates the origin of bipolar superconductivity (superconductivity under both electron and hole doping) in simple, two-dimensional electride materials.
main_result: Monolayer ZrX2 exhibits high-$T_c$ superconductivity upon electron doping, attributed to flat bands, while hole doping yields much lower $T_c$ and eventually leads to competing magnetic instabilities.
method: The research relies on first-principles calculations, including DFT, phonon calculations, and the evaluation of electron-phonon coupling (EPC) to determine superconducting critical temperatures ($T_c$).
model_or_system: The physical system is the monolayer electride ZrX2 (X = Cl, Br, I), which is modeled as a 2D semiconducting platform capable of hosting superconductivity when doped with excess electrons or holes.
key_observables: Superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$), electron-phonon coupling constant ($\lambda$), Density of States ($N(\epsilon_F)$), and magnetic moment.
important_parameters: Doping concentrations (e.g., 0.01 e/f.u. for high $T_c$), and the comparison between electron- and hole-doping regimes.
main_assumptions: The calculations assume the validity of the McMillan-Allen-Dynes formula for $T_c$ and that the structural stability can be confirmed by phonon and AIMD simulations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dependence of $T_c$ on doping for both electron and hole doping, showing the high $T_c$ dome for electrons and the suppression/instability for holes. Band structures and DOS highlight the role of flat bands near the conduction band minimum.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the material platform, calculates $T_c$ vs. doping for both electron and hole doping, analyzes the physical origin of the asymmetry (flat bands vs. VBM), and concludes by positioning ZrX2 as a tunable platform for high-$T_c$ superconductors.
why_interesting: The work directly addresses high-$T_c$ superconductivity in a controllable, engineered 2D platform, which is a major area of interest in condensed matter theory, particularly concerning the interplay between electronic structure and pairing mechanisms.
